title: Doing Social Media in the AI Era: Your Boss Is More Hopeless Than the Algorithm
dek: The real AI shock to marketing teams comes from the boss: outsourcing intuition to Claude, approving only Copilot-generated proposals, so employees disguise their ideas as Copilot screenshots to get sign-off.
why: Medium information density, but Rachel's first-hand interviews about "boss AI brain" and the Threads algorithm mechanics are industry details you won't hear elsewhere.
who: Brand social media and content marketing practitioners, MCN and creator economy investors, and anyone who wants to know how AI is changing the creative industry from inside organizations.
skip: The first two minutes of guest introductions and the Coca-Cola truck bit — jump straight to 04:06.

points.h: Bosses have outsourced their intuition to Claude
points.body: Rachel interviewed about a hundred marketers and found that the main path for AI into teams isn't tool procurement — it's the boss. A social media manager carefully makes a funny meme, sends it to the boss, and the boss drops it into Claude to ask "is this funny?" Even more absurd: some marketers discovered their boss only approves ideas that come from Copilot, so they first mock up their own ideas to look like a Copilot interface, then send that to the boss for approval. Rachel says the underlying issue is that bosses have wholesale outsourced their gut judgment to AI, while the team has no training or guardrails on how to use AI — she contrasts this with her own experience spending months learning Asana at Condé Nast.

points.h: Consumers don't hate AI, they hate being fooled
points.body: Taylor points out an overlooked fact: plenty of YouTubers now read AI-generated scripts straight to camera, and the comments still praise the "brilliant analysis, well-written script." In other words, when people don't know they're consuming AI content, they actually like it. What triggers outrage isn't AI itself but the feeling of being played. Rachel adds the explanation for this double standard: AI fruit romance memes like Fruit Love Island are low-risk memes, and nobody cares about the craft of a meme; but when a brand you pay money to uses AI to generate a menu, you suspect how much else it's cutting corners on in the product. The same person can curse brands for using AI while forwarding an AI fruit meme to a friend.

points.h: How-to creators are the first to be replaced by AI
points.body: Rachel divides creators into two categories. Those who built their following on how-to content are most at risk — from the earliest YouTube beauty tutorials onward, the democratization of media followed this path, but for questions like "how do I fix my dishwasher," AI is a better authority, and people will just ask AI. Taylor gives the example of her own mother, who recently proudly fixed her toilet using ChatGPT — previously unthinkable. The other category of creators is actually safer: those doing deep parasocial relationship content, commentary, or things that are hard to replicate can use these tools to make even better content. The test is whether the content itself is replicable.

points.h: Anti-data-center and anti-extinction people haven't allied
points.body: Taylor observes that people opposed to data centers and people worried about AI causing human extinction are two groups with completely different motivations, and they have yet to form any coherent alliance. She even jokes that they should team up, but their interests diverge too much. Her own position is clear: AI won't kill us — "it's actually very hard to kill all humans on Earth, even if we wanted to." She thinks what really deserves scrutiny is how people anthropomorphize AI and grant these products agency — especially dangerous in policy debates about accountability, because they are computer programs, not living things. She also quotes a former FTC commissioner: we survived the Black Death, and that only killed 50% of people.

points.h: AI accounts are pulling Instagram's slot machine
points.body: Taylor thinks Meta is in a tough spot because it is essentially a 2010s social media company whose influence peaked in the 2010s, while Google is better positioned than Meta. In the short term, AI's impact on platforms is about scale and speed: one AI account can post 50 times a day, which is like constantly pulling Instagram's slot machine — eventually one will hit. She checked the 20 most-viewed reels at the time, and two or three were AI-generated, and all were very new. One used a "behind-the-scenes reveal" framing to show how a film crew shoots ocean waves and how the waves destroy a house — essentially using "proof of authenticity" as a shell to create confusion. Her judgment: this is monetizing confusion, with short-term gains and terrible long-term results.

points.h: Threads is the most toxic social platform
points.body: Taylor says she recently posted hot takes calling Threads the most toxic social media platform to date, far more toxic than Twitter — "Twitter compared to Threads is a beautiful wonderland." The mechanism is that the algorithm heavily prioritizes replies, so you get dropped straight into someone's angry reply about something, which in turn feeds the algorithm and quickly escalates into groupthink-style pile-ons. She also points out that Threads' AI-generated news summaries "are just lying, making things up outright." Asked who uses Threads, her answer is her mom.

points.h: The growth secret is turning your account into a series
points.body: Asked how to grow followers in the AI era, Rachel says the accounts growing now all have a clear throughline of familiarity in their content, like they're making their own TV show. She gives the example of a restaurant chef wearing Meta glasses filming himself cooking, who grew to about 500,000 followers in two or three months under the account name Gil Holy Cooks, posting one episode a day. Taylor adds that content is becoming fully serialized across the board, and you really have to think about how to entertain people; the era of "share your life" is clearly declining, and in 2026 you shouldn't become a lifestyle influencer — people have a lot of anger toward that type.

points.h: Instagram gave an official division-of-labor chart for formats
points.body: Rachel says Instagram once shared a very useful chart with her readers explaining the purpose of each content format: carousels and reels are for reaching new audiences and get pushed to non-followers, and what the current algorithm really feeds on is non-follower views — if your content is only understandable to your own audience, the platform deems it "not entertaining enough" and withholds main traffic. Single-image posts only serve your existing audience. Stories and DMs are seen by the platform as where community happens. She also quotes Adam Mosseri on Bloomberg Screen Time: the "social" in social media is no longer about sharing family photos but about DMing friends things that remind you of them. She finds this regrettable, but it does clarify what "social" now means on social media.
